newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory cocoa arrivals seen strong early, Dec peak.
newsitem.headline: Ivory cocoa arrivals seen strong early, Dec peak.

text.p: Cocoa arrivals at Ivory Coast's main ports will be strong when the 1996/97 marketing year opens later this month, rising to a December peak, say analysts and exporters.
"The mid-crop has definitely been retained in large volumes and will be mixed in quickly as bean sizes this year were good," said one Abidjan-based private sector analyst.
"It is a late (main) crop and so arrivals will be strongest in December," he said. "It's difficult to put a figure on it, it depends on your podcount. I think it will be good."
But purchasers at one major local exporter say peak arrivals of a 1996/97 crop they estimate at 950,000 tonnes would be spread over Nov/Dec/Jan, with November slightly higher.
Main crop bean sizes were at 93 per 100 grammes compared to 110-120 a year ago, they said.

The private sector analyst said, "It is very optimistic and too early in our view." He added one pod-counter in town was leaning towards a pessimistic forecast at the lower end of the 850,000 to 930,000 tonnes range of forecasts so far of the 1996/97 main crop.
Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze recently put the total 1996/97 crop at between 891,000 and 1.009 million tonnes.

Other exporters agreed but said shipments were now grinding to a halt because it was unclear whether produce should be entered on documents as 1995/96 or the new 1996/97 marketing year crop. "There could be a small backlog by the time the season starts," one said.

Busy buying activity was reported up-country meaning some stocks had yet to be declared. Buyers licence application processing for 1996/97 will not finish until October 22 said a manager of exporters' forum GEPEX.
One exporter put first week October arrivals at 15,000 tonnes. "It's only a guess but if 20,000 arrived afterwards port stocks could be up to 40,000 tonnes at the start of the season," he said.
Figures from an official source, broken down by exporter, suggest end of season stocks could be at that level.

Caistab cocoa marketing board's private figures put total 1995/96 arrivals to the end of September at 1,331,685 tonnes, say analysts, but exporters and analysts say the figure is far too high and was more likely have been about 1,210,000 tonnes. The figures show a 70/30 percent split between 1995/96 arrivals at Abidjan and San Pedro.
Smuggling of cocoa in both directions across Ghana's border around this time of year is not expected to affect arrival volumes despite about a 40 CFA price differential at the border.
A pod counter returning from an up-country tour said he had seen cocoa smuggled in from Ghana ahead of that country's 1996/97 season price announcement, made on Tuesday.

"The volumes are too small to have an effect on arrivals," he said. "Some Ivory cocoa might now be smuggled in the opposite direction as there is still an attractive price differential," but the effect would also be negligible, he added.

Ghanaian cocoa has in the past been smuggled into Ivory Coast ahead of Ghana's Cocobod marketing board annual producer price setting. In Ghana farmers delivering to buying stations have to wait for the price announcement before being paid.
Some choose to cross the border and sell at Ivory Coast's lower price of 315 CFA per kilo, against Ghana's new price set this week of about 366 CFA, or 36,000 cedis per 30 kg load.
"There is nothing we can do until the season opens," said one exporter.
